Vanguard: Founded in 1975 by John Bogle, the pioneer of low-cost index investing. Structurally unusual: Vanguard is owned by its own funds, which are owned by their shareholders, rather than by outside stockholders — a structure it credits for its consistently rock-bottom fees. One of the two largest ETF issuers in the world by assets.
BlackRock: The world's largest asset manager overall, with trillions in assets across active and passive strategies. Its iShares brand pioneered the modern US ETF structure in 1996 and remains the largest ETF issuer by assets. Publicly traded (NYSE: BLK), led by CEO Larry Fink; the firm's size and political visibility (ESG-investing debates, state-level pension divestment fights) occasionally draws scrutiny separate from any individual fund's holdings.
State Street: Part of State Street Corporation, a Boston-based custody bank and asset manager. Its SPDR ETF business created SPY in 1993 — the first ETF listed in the US — and remains the third-largest ETF issuer globally, with particular strength in gold, sector, and institutional-focused funds.
Invesco: A global, publicly traded asset manager (NYSE: IVZ) with a diversified fund lineup spanning smart-beta, thematic, and factor-based ETFs. Best known for QQQ, one of the most heavily traded single ETFs in the world and the dominant vehicle for Nasdaq-100 exposure.
Charles Schwab: Better known as a major US discount brokerage, Schwab entered the ETF business with a lineup of ultra-low-cost, brokerage-integrated funds aimed at cost-conscious retail investors. Its dividend and core-index ETFs are frequently used as commission-free building blocks inside Schwab brokerage accounts.
